problems.description: 5 PEP8 violations reported (convention score 0.77): test_app.py and test_integration.py use non-PascalCase class names, and module-level constants in test_app.py, test_integration.py, and transports.py are not UPPER_CASE.
ClientRegistry uses threading.RLock inside an asyncio server; the registry is only accessed from the event loop, so the lock is unnecessary, and a contended threading lock could block the loop.
Broadcast via _send_many awaits each send sequentially with no per-client backpressure handling; one slow receiver can stall delivery to all other clients on the single event loop.
The wire protocol requires the client to supply a timestamp and exact key set {type, payload, timestamp}; strict set-equality validation rejects any extension and lets clients forge timestamps.

strengths: Greenfield code directly targets the notification_service story spec: an async WebSocket real-time notification server with a /health HTTP endpoint.

Clean modular layering: thread-safe ClientRegistry, NotificationServer, message validation, and routing are cleanly separated with modern typed signatures (from __future__ import annotations, str | None).
Solid async lifecycle handling — ConnectionClosed caught, client always removed in finally.
SonarQube signal is positive: bugs +0, smells -2, duplications +0.0%.
Improves on the seed app, which contained a latent data inconsistency (inserting status='done' while returning 'pending').
commit_reviews.summary: Strong architectural fit for the notification_service story — a well-structured, typed, bug-free async WebSocket server that improves on the seed — with minor convention violations concentrated in test files and transports.py (convention score 0.77), plus small async-design nits around threading and sequential broadcast.

problems.description: Channel cleanup logic is duplicated between ClientRegistry.remove() and unsubscribe() (iterate channels, discard client_id, delete empty sets); a shared _prune_channel helper would remove the drift risk.

5 convention violations scored at 0.77 (PascalCase classes and UPPER_CASE module constants in test_app.py, test_integration.py, transports.py); those flagged in app.py-adjacent test files were touched by this commit's valid_message() edit.

Direct messages silently drop when the target is not subscribed to the channel (is_subscribed() gate returns early with no system error message), unlike the existing 'client not found' path which surfaces feedback.

strengths: Extends the existing lock-protected ClientRegistry pattern consistently: new channel state follows the same RLock discipline as _clients, including correct pruning on client remove().
Validation is centralized and thorough for the new fields: channel must be a non-empty string, and subscribe/unsubscribe require it — keeping the message contract explicit.
HTTP endpoints (health, /channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers) share a single _json_response helper with consistent status/reason handling, improving on the inline response code.
New behavior is tested (valid_message() extended with channel param and additional test coverage), matching the repo's pytest discipline.
subscribe/unsubscribe are handled as local state transitions that return early, keeping the async fan-out path (_send_many) unchanged for existing message types.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-structured channel subscription feature that faithfully extends the existing registry/validation/send patterns with +0 bugs and smells (per SonarQube), offset only by rising cognitive complexity in _route() and minor test-file convention violations reflected in the 0.77 score.

problems.description: 5 convention violations per static analysis: module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in transports.py, and classes-should-be-PascalCase plus module-level-constants-should-be-UPPER_CASE in test_app.py and test_integration.py.

MessageStore performs synchronous sqlite3 I/O on the asyncio event loop (check_same_thread=False + threading.Lock); GET /messages and persistence writes can block the loop under load. Cognitive complexity +47 and +2 Sonar smells corroborate the added complexity.

The Backbone seam (InMemoryBackbone/RedisBackbone) is a sensible precursor, but Session 4's spec later extracts a WebSocket Transport interface with a different shape (on_connect/on_disconnect/send_message/broadcast); the two abstractions will need reconciliation and the InMemoryBackbone duplicates the full state-management surface of RedisBackbone.

strengths: Faithful to Session 3 spec: Redis pub/sub backbone, Redis-backed connection state, SQLite message history with GET /messages?limit&offset, and REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL env config all present.
Backbone seam with InMemoryBackbone fallback gives a Redis-free test path while RedisBackbone keeps prod semantics; pipelined multi-key updates in remove_client/subscribe are clean.
Existing message format/helper and supported types preserved, plus new integration tests (test_integration.py) added without breaking prior tests.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong, spec-compliant Session 3 integration — Redis pub/sub backbone, SQLite persistence, and a testable backbone seam — only dinged by 5 minor naming conventions and blocking SQLite calls on the event loop; no flag on the +47 cognitive complexity since the backbones are straightforward.

problems.description: Transport seam is half-abstracted: NotificationServer.handler still accepts ServerConnection and raises RuntimeError for non-WebSocket transports, yet _route reaches into transport internals (self.clients.subscribe/snapshot) directly instead of going through the transport API — connection lifecycle is split between server and transport.

Speculative abstraction: BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport/create_transport exist with only a single WebSocket implementation, so the +213/-104 line refactor adds indirection with no second consumer to justify it.

Type-safety regression: handle_message and _route take sender: Any, replacing the concrete ServerConnection type, and transport.bind(self) introduces a bidirectional server<->transport circular reference.
Cognitive complexity increased by +9 and smells by +1 for a refactor whose stated purpose is simplification — a discrepancy between the intent and the measured outcome worth flagging.

Measured convention score 0.77 with 5 violations; the commit introduces a module-level constant violation in the new transports.py, and PascalCase/UPPER_CASE violations are flagged in test_app.py and test_integration.py.

strengths: Cleanly separates WebSocket-specific concerns (ClientRegistry, connection lifecycle, send) from the core NotificationServer, enabling non-WebSocket transports and socket-free testing.
Good typing hygiene: collections.abc.Awaitable, from __future__ import annotations, and removal of now-unused imports (uuid, ConnectionClosed).
create_transport factory driven by a TRANSPORT env var is a reasonable DI seam that preserves the existing backbone/store/message() patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound transport-abstraction direction undermined by a half-completed seam — the server still couples directly to the registry while advertising transport-agnosticism, and measured complexity rose +9 — making the refactor net neutral.

problems.description: The new index on (channel, timestamp, id) is partially defeated: history() and delete_older_than() wrap timestamp in julianday(), so SQLite cannot use the index for the range predicate and will scan all rows for the channel. ISO-8601 timestamps compare lexicographically and would make the range query index-friendly.

InMemoryBackbone.rate_limit_exceeded rebuilds the entire _rate_limits dict (O(n) sweep) on every request; acceptable at this scale but unbounded growth is only pruned per request. A lazily-pruned approach or scheduled cleanup would be cleaner.
_positive_int_env swallows the original ValueError message and re-raises an identical generic message for both parse failures and non-positive values, losing diagnostic detail.
No test additions visible in the diff for the new /history endpoint, rate limiting (both backbones), or TTL cleanup, while the SonarQube cognitive complexity (+21) adds untested branches.

All 5 measured convention violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE constants) are located in test_app.py, test_integration.py, and transports.py — files not modified by this commit. The 0.77 convention score reflects pre-existing violations, not this diff.

strengths: Rate limiting added symmetrically to both InMemoryBackbone and RedisBackbone, honoring the existing abstraction seam rather than special-casing one backend.
MessageStore.history and delete_older_than extend the established storage method pattern, reusing the same lock discipline and row-shaping as list().
The /history route mirrors the existing /messages routing, pagination validation, and JSON response conventions.
Clean env-driven configuration with validated parsing and sane defaults (RATE_LIMIT=100/min, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS=7).
Cleanup task lifecycle is correctly managed — created on start, cancelled and awaited on close.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured feature commit that extends existing backbone/store/routing patterns correctly, but adds minor technical debt (function-wrapped timestamp queries defeating the new index, +21 cognitive complexity) and the 0.77 convention score reflects violations in unmodified test/transport files rather than this diff's app.py changes.

compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the Flask seed wholesale rather than reusing any of it; acceptable for greenfield, but the git diff shows the entire 128-line app.py replaced, so no seed structure survived to constrain or inform later sessions.

Session 3 routes even locally-connected clients through Redis pub/sub via a self-loopback (the server publishes to 'notifications' and its own listener re-delivers), coupling local delivery to Redis liveness; the origin/_instance_id guard was added but never checked, so a mid-run Redis failure silently kills delivery with no local fallback.

Per-instance SQLite persistence means /messages and /history reflect only the local instance's writes, so 'integration' (multi-server scale-out) never delivers globally-consistent history — a limitation that persists through sessions 4 and 5.

Subscription state is kept in two places (in-memory channels dicts plus Redis sets in session 3), creating dual bookkeeping that must be kept in sync across every connect/disconnect/subscribe/unsubscribe path.

Session 3's send_direct path only falls back to local delivery when Redis is absent; when Redis is present it returns True for remote targets but offers no delivery acknowledgement, a semantics ambiguity retained by later sessions.
key_decisions: Session 1: discard the Flask seed and build a dependency-light asyncio WebSocket server (websockets lib + hand-rolled asyncio HTTP for /health), with UUID client IDs and lock-protected client registry.
Session 1: canonical envelope {type, payload, timestamp[, channel]} with a MESSAGE_TYPES whitelist — the extensible wire contract every later session plugged into.
Session 2: channel subscribe/unsubscribe protocol plus /channels and /channels/<name>/subscribers HTTP introspection endpoints.
Session 3: Redis pub/sub fan-out for multi-instance scale-out combined with SQLite message persistence and a paginated /messages endpoint.
Session 4: extract BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport into transport.py, decoupling socket I/O from notification routing state so the server core becomes transport-agnostic.

Session 5: cross-cutting operations — Redis-backed (with local fallback) rate limiting that returns a graceful error rather than dropping messages, TTL-based message retention with an hourly cleanup loop, and a /history endpoint with since-filter and has_more cursor pagination.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 established a clean, fully-tested core (unique client IDs, broadcast/direct/system routing, health endpoint) as a dependency-light asyncio server; Session 2 extended it with channels that slotted cleanly into the existing envelope and routing model; Session 3 added a credible scale-out story via Redis pub/sub and SQLite persistence while adding five integration tests; Session 4 was a genuine structural refactor that shrank the core by extracting a transport abstraction with all prior tests still green; and Session 5 layered on cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, TTL cleanup, history pagination) with two additional tests. The final state is a well-layered ~440-line server with a 242-line test suite, all 10 tests passing, and no visible regression or backtracking anywhere in the arc.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, steadily-improving five-session arc (greenfield → features → integration → refactor → cross-cutting ops) where every decision built on the prior session's wire format and state model, ending with a clean, well-tested, operationally complete notification server.
